title: Why Your Time-Out Doesn't Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that time-out frequently fails not because of the consequence itself but because teachers misunderstand its actual mechanism, sometimes turning it into a shame-based punishment that breeds resentment rather than reflection. His core claim is that time-out only works as leverage -- it requires a classroom students genuinely enjoy being part of, so that removal from it feels like the loss of something valued rather than an escape from something unpleasant. He frames the goal explicitly as widening the experiential gap between being in class and being in time-out until even challenging students actively prefer to avoid the latter, and states plainly that he wants his own classroom gratifying enough that students despise time-out by comparison. He's careful to distinguish this from punishment, lecturing, or persuasion, arguing instead that the entire SCM philosophy is built around using natural human inclination -- wanting to belong to something good -- to get students to choose good behavior on their own, which he argues is the only version of the choice that actually sticks.
points: Time-out commonly fails because teachers turn it into shame-based punishment rather than a place of reflection, which breeds resentment instead of change.
Time-out only functions as real leverage when the regular classroom is genuinely enjoyable enough that removal feels like a loss, not a relief.
States the explicit goal of making the classroom gratifying enough that students actively despise being sent to time-out by comparison.
Distinguishes this from lecturing, scolding, or persuasion -- the aim is for good behavior to be the student's own choice, since only self-chosen change actually sticks.
quotes: Understanding time-out, its purpose and function, is key to its effectiveness.
It’s not a dunce-cap punishment or place for students to feel shame, which only causes resentment and more misbehavior.
Rather, time-out must be a place of reflection and determination to do better.

To ensure this is the case, you must create a classroom your students enjoy being part of. This is essential. Because if your students don’t like you or sitting in your classroom, then time-out won’t work.
Personally, I want to make my classroom so gratifying that they despise time-out.
When it comes from them, when it’s their choice—that just so happens to be inspired by the classroom conditions you’ve created—then it sticks.
